records.text: 30 April 2026 Myth Buster Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG Myth 4: Sell in May is a global phenomenon. False: Historically, "Sell in May" with cash proved less effective than a simple Buy and Hold strategy for US equities, delivering 9.3% versus 10.4% p.a. since 1973. Conversely, investing in US Treasuries during the summer period boosted the strategy to a 12.0% p.a. return, outperforming Buy and Hold. Nevertheless, the success of the strategy again comes with a critical caveat: it is highly sensitive to timing. Omitting the exceptional years (1998, 2001, and 2002) would have significantly reduced its annual performance to just 10.5%. The strategy’s hit ratio in the US is even more disappointing than in Europe, beating the market in only 22 out of 53 years. Last year, when US equities gained 14% from May to September, while US Treasuries only returned 3%, the strategy would have led to an 11% underperformance against Buy and Hold. records.text: European Economics 27 April 2026 Citi Research 3 This takes us back to what is by now a familiar discussion: how should and how will the Governing Council react when real and nominal data diverge and the range of plausible outcomes is very wide? Our way to answer that remains driven by an observation we made repeatedly: policy decisions are not determined only by what policy-makers want to achieve, but also by what they seek to avoid. Understanding which risks they fear most often provides the key to anticipating their course of action. Incidentally, this strikes us as perfectly reasonable. The mandate of central banks is essentially to guard the economy against dangers, so the notion that their reaction function consists in minimising a loss function is entirely rational. If we approach the issue in this way, it seems equally logical to expect that the Governing Council will not take any policy action at the forthcoming meeting on 30 April, and this is indeed our (consensual) expectation. records.text: 1 Insights Classification: ComplimentaryMaterial April FOMC: It’s not goodbye, it’s see you later April 29, 2026 Stand my ground. The two clear takeaways from the FOMC meetings are the following: First, Chairman Powell confirmed he will be staying on as governor given the unprecedented legal attacks on the Fed. Powell did not commit to a firm departure date saying he will leave when he believes it appropriate. Considering his term does not end until January 31, 2028, he could stay on for another 21 months, which would mean, bar an unexpected departure, President Trump would not get a new nomination for nearly two years. At the press conference Powell reiterated he believes rates are at the high end of neutral, meaning that unless energy inflation becomes entrenched or the labor market cools materially, he is likely content with policy stasis. Reading between the lines. The second takeaway is a clear lack of consensus at the Fed as the FOMC voted to hold policy unchanged in an 8-4 decision. Any degree of dissent is unusual, occurring at only 36% of meetings going back to 1936, making 4 dissents a rarity – something that has not occurred since 1992 (Figure 1). Miran, in keeping with his streak, dissented in favor of a cut, while the other three dissents were due to more hawkish views. records.text: ab 27 April 2026 Global Research European Economic Perspectives European inflation monthly: April preview April inflation preview across Europe Higher energy prices to push inflation higher in the Eurozone and Switzerland. Inflation in the UK and Sweden is likely to ease temporarily in April. Eurozone HICP: Headline +0.4pp to 3%; core -0.4pp to 1.9% Similar to March, we expect another energy-led inflation jump in April with headline inflation up 0.4pp to 3% y/y (out on 30 April). We project energy prices to rise 5.3% m/ m following +7% m/m in March, pushing annual energy inflation up by 8.2pp to 13.3% y/y. In contrast, we expect core inflation to temporarily drop 0.4pp to 1.9% y/y, solely driven by a 0.7pp drop in services inflation to 2.5% y/y due to the earlier timing of Easter compared to last year. Importantly, we expect this drop to reverse in May, when we foresee services inflation bouncing back to 2.9% y/y. In contrast, goods inflation is likely to remain unchanged at 0.5% y/y. Outside of core, food inflation is likely to ease 0.1pp to 2.3% y/y. At the country level, we expect inflation to rise in Germany (+0.2pp to 3% y/y), France (+0.4pp to 2.4% y/y) and Italy (+1.2pp to 2.8% y/y). Inflation in Spain is likely to remain unchanged (at 3.4%) and ease in the Netherlands (-0.5pp to 2.1%). records.text: 4 Liquid Insight | 27 April 2026 FX: Ceasefire > FOMC The April FOMC is unlikely to be a major event for the USD, but risks skew marginally bullish, to the extent that Chair Powell reiterates his more hawkish tone from March. Recall that at the March FOMC, comments in the press conference emphasized war- induced upside inflation risks, while also downplaying concerns in the labor market. Since then, oil prices are roughly unchanged on net, and labor market indicators have improved. However, the FX market has been more captivated by optimism over a ceasefire in Iran, and the recent relative data improvement hasn’t translated into USD strength. (Exhibit 3) In terms of any forward guidance any revealed discussion of hikes would be a surprise, likely sparking a USD rally. On the other hand, denying any material discussion took place could weigh on the USD slightly. Stepping back, the USD has been remarkably range-bound over the past year. (Exhibit 4) With the Fed priced to be on-hold for an extended period, any material and prolonged range break will likely need to coincide with a more significant Fed repricing, in either direction. Over time, this could come (to the downside) in the presumed Warsh regime, if he is able to steer the committee towards a more dovishly biased stance. On the other side, we still see the bar for hikes as asymmetrically higher (than cuts) in this current environment. Since the last refunding announcement in February, there have been a number of updates to the fiscal outlook. First, the Supreme Court overturned the use of IEEPA for broad tariffs, and the CIT then ordered the US Customs and Border Protection Office (CBP) to create a system to refund eligible importers for the $166bn of IEEPA tariffs that were paid. CBP created a portal to accept refund applications, and estimated in court filings that roughly $127bn would be eligible for refunds electronically, at an estimated timeline of 60-90 days from the time of application. We expect roughly $30bn of refunds to be paid in FY26, and $90bn in FY27, with the first wave of refunds paid over June and July. To the extent Treasury anticipates this increased financing need into the summer, we expect T-bill issuance to ramp higher in anticipation, to avoid the TGA dipping below the 5-day minimum as refunds are paid out. Long-end bonds to be supported by WGBI flows: The long end of the curve is a different story. Two opposing forces are at play: strong growth and fiscal stimulus are pushing rates higher, while USD50bn inflows related to WGBI inclusion are keeping a lid on rates, especially towards every month end. We expect this tug-of-war in long-end rates to continue. In our view, the majority of the growth momentum and fiscal impact will be concentrated in the 5y segment of the curve. Recall that TBAC introduced a stylized “buyback score” framework last year, which utilizes offer-to-max ratios, yield dispersion around a fitted Treasury curve, and a measure of liquidity preference based on on-the-run/off-the-run valuations across each buyback maturity bucket (Figure 5B u y b a c k s a p p e a r t o b e w o r k i n g a s i n t e n d e d a n d w e d o n o t e x p e c t a n y c h a n g e s t o o p e r a t i o n s i z e s t o b e a n n o u n c e d i n M a y ). Looking across these measures, liquidity has improved across most tenors since February, and no longer appears elevated in the very front end. The one exception is the long end, where offer-to-max ratios increased in the 20- to 30-year sector over the last three months. Thus, we assume the buyback program remains at its current size, with up to $38bn of liquidity support purchases per quarter and cash management buybacks of up to $150bn per year. With a portion of these operations likely to go unfilled, buybacks should add ~$240bn of financing needs in 2026. If market liquidity deteriorates more than we expect, Treasury could make modest tweaks to liquidity management operations over time. Regarding the war, we think Powell will note both the upside risks to inflation and the downside risks to the labor market and growth. But which way will he lean? If his comments mirror Daly’s (mentioned above), markets would read that as very hawkish. Powell could get asked about the pickup in the labor data. We think he’ll probably caution against over-reacting to a few data points, and state that the broad labor data have been soft but stable. A dovish response would note that wage inflation has been weakening. A more hawkish answer would lean into downside risks to the u-rate, even if they are mostly due to slowing labor supply. Powell will likely get a question about Kevin Warsh’s Fed Chair nomination hearing. We think he’ll refrain from commenting unless he’s asked about specific policy proposals. For example, if pressed on Warsh’s preference for trimmed-mean and median inflation over the core PCE, Powell might express an open mind to alternate inflation metrics, but emphasize the importance of not cherry picking.

records.text: FOCUS F O C U S 28/04/2026 1 A key opportunity to signal term premium relief: The US administration considers Treasury yields a key barometer of affordability, given their influence on mortgage rates. As the next few months are likely to be the main home buying season of 2026, the May refunding will be the administration’s main opportunity to provide mortgage rate relief and address housing affordability before this year’s mid-term elections. At February’s refunding, the Treasury indicated that coupon size increases were being considered. However, a focus on “structural demand trends” hinted that any coupon increases might only be in the front-end, alongside T-bills continuing to do the heavy lifting. Coincidentally, the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee (TBAC) recommended in its first charge that increases in shorter-maturity coupon issuance would lower volatility without much increase in expected interest costs. This addresses concerns that relying wholly on T- bills and leaving coupons unchanged increases rollover risk and pushes the T-bill share well above 25% in the next few years. Our baseline is for Treasury to maintain its "T-bill and chill" strategy while also increasing coupon auction sizes at the front-end and intermediate sector – after the next few quarters. Back in the 2000s, an SPD-led government pushed through far-reaching labour market and welfare reforms. The speech can be seen as the kick-off for structural reforms to be shaped until the July parliamentary summer break. n First reform package to be announced over the course of April/May. A first milestone is April 29, when the headline figures for the 2027 budget are scheduled to be presented and the cabinet is set to agree on a health care reform proposal. An income tax proposal is set to follow shortly thereafter. The planned reforms will increase work incentives (by lowering the income tax for small and middle incomes) and curb increases in non-wage labour costs (by keeping contributions to the statutory health insurance stable). n Short-term macroeconomic impact to be limited, but household and corporate sentiment to be positively affected. New reform momentum might affect corporate and household sentiment positively at a crucial juncture, when the energy price spike has become more than a speed bump on Germany's road to recovery. We expect that this change should continue to serve as a positive tailwind for foreign demand. Foreign investors shift to TMT and the long end — Data on purchases through dealer affiliates suggests that foreign investors increased their share of purchases of TMT corporates from 17.1% in 2025 to 26.1% in 2026, while reducing Financials exposure from 53.8% to 39%. Demand for 15y+ supply also increased to 44.1% of total purchases in 2026 from 23.7% in 2025. These changes in allocations are not explained purely by changes in issuance composition in the past few months and suggest a broader thematic driven reallocation. Demand from abroad continues to outpace growth in the market — When looking at foreign demand inflows as a percent of net supply and foreign demand growth relative to market growth, both are at historically elevated levels and have increased over the past months. This pushes back against the notion that elevated geopolitical and trade tensions since February 2025 would dampen foreign demand. The Fed is not blameless in that as it's grown, the Fed's balance sheet grown its imprimatur on the economy. Those with financial assets have benefited from it. The reason why I prefer monetary policy to use interest rates as the dominant force is, interest rates affect a far broader cross section of the economy. Interest rates get in the cracks. If we were to cut rates, then broader number of people will benefit from it versus quantitative easing, which tends to move through financial assets first. records.text: Liquid Insight | 27 April 2026 3 On the balance sheet, Powell could note that there is room for reduction in response to liquidity deregulation, but that a large majority of the committee wants to stay in an ample reserve regime. We don’t think he’ll take a strong stand on Warsh’s statement that the Fed shouldn’t own long-dated Treasuries. Finally, now that the DoJ probe has been dropped, Powell will almost certainly get asked whether he plans to stay on at the Fed as a Governor. Our best guess is that he’ll stay at least until the Supreme Court rules on the Lisa Cook case (and possibly much longer). But he might choose not to reveal his plans just yet. US rates: hawkish swan song The Fed is widely expected to keep rates steady at the April FOMC. The market is well priced for no change. Our economists expect few changes in the policy statement & see risks the Powell presser skews modestly hawkish. The April FOMC press conference could potentially be the last of Powell’s tenure. Powell’s press conference may skew slightly hawkish given upside inflation risks, solid labor & consumer spending in March, and easy financial conditions. Seasonality improves at the start of October and US equities historically see +22% returns in the 12 months following the midterms (early November). Despite some retracement, the market is still pricing in around four rate hikes from the BoK over the next year (Figure 5). The uncertainty around the BoK's future actions, volatility in the currency, and the transmission of inflationary risks are contributing to the persistent volatility in rates. It is important, however, to underline that this change does not reflect a strong conviction that this is the rate path that will materialise. We are in a situation where the range of possible outcomes remains wide. Over the next few months, the most critical input into the deliberations of the Governing Council of the ECB ought to be the length of closure of the Strait of Hormuz. We have no means of making informed guesses on this, and neither do central bankers. So, like them, we must be willing to amend our view – possibly significantly – as political decisions and military developments unfold. With this in mind, our change of baseline projection reflects essentially two considerations: first, it seems to us that – compared with a few weeks ago – the risk of a prolonged disruption of oil and gas shipment from the Persian Gulf must have risen. It is not just a matter of observing that the Straits remains closed so far. We find it also more difficult to believe in a rapid and lasting re-opening, in a context where communication by belligerents does not seem particularly consistent over time. We also continue to expect an increased emphasis on defence, energy autonomy and technological catching up to push governments to increase public investment, possibly very substantially. This ought to also contribute to raising inflation and neutral rates. While we did and continue to expect this shift to materialise in 2027 and beyond rather than in 2026, it is relevant to monetary policy in 2026. Given the long transmission lags of monetary policy, if the Governing Council has cause to expect this type of fiscal expansion next year, that reduces considerably the arguments in favour of reversing any rate hike. What we mean here, in essence, is that we would likely see rate hikes in the summer as premature, rather than completely misguided. It is for those reasons that our baseline projections now assume two rate hikes in June and July, followed by a long plateau rather than a reversal. We underline once again that a projection of that sort in a context like the current one really is very fragile to political decisions in Europe (e.g. on defence spending) and even more so outside of Europe (on the conduct of the war in Iran). records.text: 27 April 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 7 3) Income tax reform - details have to be ironed out The government has found a political agreement to reduce the tax burden for small and middle-income earners, but details still have to be ironed out over the course of May. FinMin Klingbeil is expected to present a legislative proposal by the end of May, with many details unclear yet. According to media reports,2 the reform could include these elements: n Increase of the basic tax-free allowance, currently at EUR 12,348, by EUR 500 or EUR 1,000. Such hikes are done regularly and are undisputed. A DIW proposal also suggests raising the initial tax rate from 14% to 19%.3 n Slight flattening of the tax curve for small and middle-income earners by increasing the threshold from which the top tax rate applies to EUR 80,000 or EUR 90,000 (from a taxable income of EUR 69,879 currently). The CDU and SPD have been advocating for this. n Raising the top tax rate from currently 42% to up to 49% and abolishing the solidarity surcharge. Currently, this surcharge of 5.5% has to be paid by people whose tax amount exceeds EUR 20,350 (single household, EUR 40,700 for couples). While the SPD is in favour of hiking the top tax rate, the CDU is opposing this but could ultimately accept this if the solidarity surcharge is removed. Relief: Investors pushed policy expectations to their heights during the worst of the conflict, so they have naturally faded a bit as we have moved to a less violent phase. This also marked a USD top, with real money broadly buying everything other than the dollar (as shown in Figure 1). We also noticed that currency returns have been somewhat correlated with the degree of policy hikes that investors were willing to fade (Figure 3). The USD is invariably part of this move, although we attribute the potential reduction in policy mistakes across the G-10 as a tertiary benefit. These relationships ultimately push against IRP, demonstrating that the extent of current uncertainty and the ability for long established relationships to break down. Terminal: Recent stability in policy rates has come with a notably higher terminal value, which is 35-70 bps above levels before the conflict. These levels seem to be holding, with overall rates volatility compressing like most asset classes. Cause or effect, the correlation between rates and FX vol is clear, as shown in Figure 4. We think that this consolidation is sustainable and expect lower rates and currency vol once the current round of CB meetings sunset. As such we are leaving our portfolio unchanged this week, with a risk on bias that favours commodity currencies at the expense of the European currencies and the USD. In this report, we discuss how equity investors value long-term growth. The perceived threat of AI disruption has increased investor focus on the "terminal• value" of many equities. Based on a 10-year dividend discount model, we estimate that the terminal value of the S&P 500 represents roughly 75% of its equity value today, near the highest level in 25 years. We es timate that every 1 pp change in long-term growth rate affects the current S&P 500 enterprise value by 15%. records.text: Second part of report title Sources: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas Europe still a bright spot for metals demand as infrastructure spending increases: While demand growth has been sluggish in the US and China in aggregate, the story has been more positive for Europe. We currently project about 4% demand growth in Europe this year following three years of contraction. However, we do see challenges ahead, notably due to the possibility of sustained high energy prices negatively impacting European budgets and growth in 2026. European auto sector outlook still challenging but some signs of improvement visible: Auto registrations showed modest growth through 2025 in Europe, up 1.5% y/y. Consensus expectations are for this to jump to about 2.9% in 2026. More importantly for metals demand, order intake for European auto manufacturers improved through H2 2025, thanks to auto inventories being drawn down, and the positive trend has continued into 2026. records.text: Second part of report title 2 Copper: Pricing scarcity in a time of plenty KEY MESSAGES Lifting our copper-price forecasts despite weak fundamentals: We raise our 2026 and 2027 copper forecasts despite clearly weak fundamentals, as funds’ interest in copper continues to support prices well above fundamentally justified levels. Indeed, we now expect prices to surge on moves towards peace in the Middle East. Our base case is for prices to jump to about USD14,000/t in Q2 2026. No refined copper shortages, deep contangos likely to be longer lasting: We see the refined copper oversupply in 2025 being sustained in 2026 and 2027. We estimate the surplus in the copper market last year was about 900kt, with much of the excess being drawn into the US on import-tariff fears. We expect current high prices to prompt buyer strikes and demand destruction, which, along with improving primary and secondary supply, will drive much-needed price correction in H2 2026. Pricing difference driven by speculative interest: The surge of non-commodity- specialist investors’ interest in copper from December 2025 to January 2026 has, in our view, significantly altered the nature of copper pricing. Currently, the copper market appears to be pricing in extreme shortages despite historically high visible inventories as funds buy into false narratives of booming copper demand from AI data centres or a lack of copper supply growth. We do not see this speculative disconnect as sustainable in the longer term. F

The 10y level is less important than inflation Since the start of 2025, the rates-spread correlation in both US IG and HY has remained firmly negative with all-in-yield-buyers, particularly in IG, stepping in to keep spreads near historic tights. Historically, there have been very few periods where the rates-spread correlation has been sustainably positive with both moving higher – over the past 20y, we have essentially only seen this dynamic in the lead-up to the GFC, briefly during the 2013 Fed ‘taper tantrum’, as well as in the 2022 inflation shock. The common thread between these three episodes was either 1) a monetary policy regime change (2013) or 2) a rise in longer-term inflation expectations (2008/2022) which derailed both rates and spreads. We have found that over a long-term lookback, changes in the level of 10y rates explain less than 10% of the monthly variation in credit spreads – far lower than inflation expectations which explain over a third – with no clear cutoff in yield level to flip the rates-spread correlation positive outside of the highly restrictive (6%+) levels seen in the late 1990’s. records.text: 6 Euro Area Watch | 27 April 2026 Rates Edvard Davidsson MLI (UK) edvard.davidsson@bofa.com MEF: flexible approach in pursuit of demand With redemptions still elevated, a legacy of the shorter-tenor issuance profile during the Covid years, gross supply is set to remain sizeable. And with the fiscal path to debt sustainability still narrow, we expect the MEF (Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance) to continue being an increasingly proactive issuer, seeking where demand provides the most attractive funding opportunities. First, we see growing scope for issuance via alternatives to regular coupon auctions, such as linkers, private placements and USD-denominated bonds. Following a successful syndication that attracted strong foreign participation, syndications are also likely to remain an important issuance channel through the remainder of 2026. Second, due to the steepness of the curve and lack of demand, the MEF appears reluctant to materially increase supply in the long end (20–30 years). Instead, the 7–8 year and 15-year sectors offer more attractive issuance yields and greater depth of demand. Positioning: investors remain hopeful The prevailing view across Italy’s political spectrum is that debt sustainability remains an important consideration, but that some of the more alarmist narratives are overstated. For now, market behaviour seems to indicate only modest concern. We do not see the typical curve-flattening pressures that often accompany acute Italian credit concerns

records.text: elp Forecast Spot Prices?2 The paper finds that commodity futures prices are difficult to beat as forecasts of future spot prices when evaluated out of sample, even though they often fail standard in-sample efficiency tests. It argues that futures-based forecasts perform as well as or better than simple benchmarks like random walks across a range of commodities and forecast horizons. Overall, the key takeaway is that commodity futures embed useful forward-looking information and are a robust, low-cost forecasting tool for policymakers and practitioners. Ellwanger & Snudden (2021): Futures Prices Are Useful Predictors of the Spot Price of Crude Oil3 This paper argues that more recently, futures have become better predictors. Post-2005 data show significant forecast accuracy gains: futures curves at 1–5y horizons outperform the no- change benchmark. Also, incorporating end-of-month futures prices (instead of monthly averages) improves short-term forecast accuracy by ~40%. This suggests market efficiency improved in recent years, though risk premia still exist. Cortazar et al. (2022): Time‑Varying Term Structure of Oil Risk Premia4 Using a multi-factor term structure model calibrated to both futures prices and survey-based expectations, the authors show that oil risk premia are sizable, time-varying, and decline with maturity (higher and more volatile at the short end). 30 April 2026 13 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: In no rush

records.text: nd is towards the top end of neutral now. The weakness in our reasoning is that it places little weight on inflation expectations, or the risk of de-anchoring thereof. This takes us away from the input into the Governing Council discussion (the data) and toward a discussion of how the Governing Council processes that input (the reaction function). Faced with the same data, the policy reaction depends on where the burden of proof lies. We have many times argued that with the same mandate, central bankers can have very different policy inclinations depending on how much weight they place on inflation expectations and how asymmetric is their aversion for error. The ECB’s monetary policy strategy statement affirms that the Governing Council considers negative and positive deviations of inflation from the target as equally undesirable. That may be true in theory, but in practice, individual members will have a more pronounced aversion for deviation on one side or the other, depending on assumptions they make about the consequences. Introduction One of the more notable exchanges in Kevin Warsh’s nomination hearing (see “Market's first Warsh -ach test ”) was that his preferred inflation gauges were “trimmed averages” that “take out all of the tail risks, all of the one -off items” to get at the “generalized change in prices”. In this piece, we look at these alternative measures of inflation and compare them to the more traditional gauges such as headline or core . In particular, we focus on whether trimmed -mean or median inflation measures are indeed superior measures of trend inflation. The rationale for looking at these alternative inflation measures is similar to that for core. Excluding food and energy prices is justified, not because these prices are unimportant – quite the contrary – but because these items have their own idiosyncratic drivers and any large moves up or down are likely to be short-lived or “transitory”. As such, core inflation has often been found to be more informative than headline about trend inflation in certain regimes. records.text: Euro Area: Rates Strategy Hike another day The conflict and oil prices continue to be the key driver for EUR rates, making directional and curve trades challenging. The ECB held fire in April but left the door wide open for a hike in June, with the duration of the conflict a key variable for the policy path. Slipping and sliding on oil (again). The EUR rates market remains firmly in the grip of the Middle-East conflict and by extension, the evolution of oil prices. With no sign of an imminent and credible de-escalation, the push higher in Brent prices has weighed on the front-end rates again this week, flattening the curve and pushing breakevens higher. The conflict aside, the market had to digest a fair few central bank meetings and key data points, specifically the consumer inflation expectations and HICP prints in the euro area. The latter clearly showed that the conflict is already starting to have an impact (see Figure 3 for the data dashboard) and the ECB will take these and the upcoming prints on board when they meet again in June. President Lagarde delivered a balanced press conference, keeping all options open as expected but clearly hinting that the next move is higher policy rates if the conflict persists. Our economists continue to expect two 25bp rate hikes from the ECB in June and September, respectively. From this starting point, and with only one further inflation print before the June meeting in addition to the April release, it is hard to envisage the data u-turning convincingly enough to induce the board to hike before the August meeting, in our view. Clearly, the continuation of the US–Iran hostilities - and the associated stickiness in elevated energy prices - is an adverse development. But, as discussed above, so too are the inflation and growth data observed since the last meeting. A lower starting point for inflation gives the Board more room to wait, a point several members have emphasised since the last meeting. It is also worth noting that, at its peak, the halving of VAT on food is expected to subtract around 0.7pp from CPIF y/y, according to the Riksbank. By way of comparison, even a doubling of energy inflation in the near term - from around 9% y/y in March to 20% - would only just be sufficient to offset that effect. Given the demonstrated resilience of the European (and global) economy to recurrent shocks recently, and given incentives for private investment to remain relatively robust (in a context of technological and geopolitical revolution), we are not currently expecting an environment comparable to 2011. The second major different between 2011 and now is that the ECB hiked rates then in the context of general downtrend in inflation and real rates. Now, we see the trend as going in the other direction. Back then, Europe was adopting austerity policies that increased a pre-existing shortage of demand relative to supply globally, and of investment relative to savings. The former contributed to disinflation, the latter to ever falling neutral real rates. Those forces would eventually force the ECB (and other central banks) to reach the lower bound of interest rates and experiment with unconditional forward guidance, negative rates and quantitative easing. records.text: : As recent data has shown, South Korea has continued to benefit from strong semiconductor exports. With AI investment trends likely to continue in our view, and chip prices remaining elevated, we expect South Korea’s current account balance to remain resilient. Additionally, we note local authorities have taken steps to address the imbalanced flow picture, which has contributed to currency weakness in recent years (MoEF, 24 December 2025). In particular, reshoring investment accounts (RIA) were implemented one month ago, and have seen significant uptake (Figure 8), likely due to the KOSPI’s strong performance relative to US equities. Alongside WGBI inflows, the National Pension Service’s strategic hedging and temporary waiver on portfolio rebalancing, and with scope for a medium-term shift in the asset allocation towards domestic assets (due to be announced in late May, in our view), we expect the portfolio flow outlook to remain supportive for the KRW. Dividend seasonality set to fade after April: We think that the recent KRW underperformance is partially related to KOSPI dividend seasonality, with overseas investors possibly repatriating dividend earnings. However, we note that KOSPI dividend payments are concentrated in April, so this dividend headwind should fade soon. records.text: policy? In this section, we explore reasons why trimmed-mean may not be strictly preferable to headline or core. Trimmed-mean can lag when inflation regimes change One clear benefit to trimmed-mean is that it is easy to communicate why certain products are being excluded on a month -by-month basis. Inflation is measured imprecisely, so excluding some of the “noise” of large moves in smaller categories (which do not necessarily have to be food or energy categories) can provide a clearer picture of the trend. However, fundamental to this is the premise that the inflation prints out in the tails are in fact noise and thus not informative about the trend. Previous Fed research has found that trimmed-mean is “more useful in low inflation environments, when the underlying signal is weak relative to the noise in the data”, but may not be able to timely capture changes in the inflation regime that information in the tails may help identify. For example, if large increases in gas prices are indicative of future cost -push energy pressures or spikes in used car prices signal extreme supply -demand imbalances that are likely to persist , then t rimmed-mean and median inflation would systematically strip out that signal. As a result, these alternative measures would rise much slower than headline or core would. What has changed is our reading of the balance of opinion and influence in the Governing Council. We have no reason at the moment to believe that, even if the energy price shock extends or intensifies, it will morph into a genuine inflation shock (by which we mean a self-fulfilling increase in prices). Compared to 2022, in particular, it seems to us that firms’ pricing power ought to be significantly lower. Back then, there existed pent-up demand that resulted from the fact that confined workers had continued to be compensated even if they did not produce. This mechanically resulted in keeping demand supported (or more precisely building up pent-up demand to be released at the point of reopening) in the face of a large cumulative shortfall in supply. What we see at the moment is very different. There is no such imbalance. Consumer sentiment appears to have been hit particularly hard, which suggests that higher direct energy costs will be accompanied by a reduction in discretionary spending (consistent with the weak reading of services PMI). If so, firms may find it much harder to pass on input costs to final consumers. That would lead to a lower transmission from energy prices to other prices, i.e. from headline to core inflation. In this context, we think perhaps the most relevant piece of information is the suggestion by the President of the European Central Bank, in the aftermath of the March meeting, that inflation expectations “have a lot do to with the memory that people (…) have of inflation” and that economic agents’ reaction function to a price shock will be informed by fresh memories of a high level of inflation. We interpret this comment to convey (1) even more emphasis on the risk of de-anchoring of expectations than we thought and (2) a lower bar for assuming that this risk is clear and present. Combined with a seemingly even larger “hawkish” constituency in the Council than we thought, we have little choice but to revise our conclusion marginally, by allowing for a more rapid tightening, if the energy price shock does not reverse fast Prepared for Cayla Buettner

To be sure, the specter of the inflation surge from 2021-22 hung over Frankfurt, but the key question is how, not if, energy prices pass through to inflation. records.text: M Idea 6 Monetary Policy and the Transition at the Fed As noted in prior research, one of the final hurdles for the market to overcome was the Fed's recent hawkish pivot on higher oil prices and the transition of its leadership from Jay Powell to Fed Chair nominee Kevin Warsh. This past week, Kevin Warsh finally appeared in front of the Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs committee. In an effort to distance himself from President Trump's influence, he framed himself as an independent, credibility-focused central banker intent on restoring a more traditional Fed. In doing so, he signaled some caution on near-term rate cuts, noting that inflation risks are not resolved. We would point out that the Treasury Secretary has also tried to give him cover on this by saying the Fed could wait to see how the near-term path of inflation evolves amid the war/oil spike before acting too soon on rate cuts. In short, based on this, there's a case to be made that we may not see rate cuts this summer unless the conflict or some other shock were to have a major impact on growth. So far that is not the case. He also criticized the post-2020 framework, noting that the Fed "missed its mark" on inflation, overused tools like QE and expanded into areas beyond its core mandate. He favors a narrower interpretation of that mandate, focusing on price stability and employment, and is open to revisiting how inflation is measured and targeted. Although we’ve only shifted Waller, Daly and Miran for now, the risk is that more dots will move up by June. Everyone we’ve heard from since the March meeting has sounded at least marginally more hawkish than before (e.g., Williams). Regarding the FOMC statement, the big question is whether it will indicate that risks to the policy path are two-sided. One way to do this would be to change the reference to “additional adjustments” to the policy rate in the forward guidance language to “any adjustments” or simply “adjustments”. This would indicate that the next move wouldn’t necessarily be in the same direction as the previous one. We do expect one change to the statement. Given the downward revisions to 4Q GDP and soft consumer spending in Jan-Feb, we think the Fed will choose to downgrade the description of economic activity from “solid” to “moderate”. We anticipate only one dissent once again, from Gov. Miran, in favor of a 25bp cut. Turning to Chair Powell’s press conference, we think he will sound moderately hawkish. For one, the data flow and balance of risks support a more hawkish stance, as discussed above. The reason for this divergence between trimmed-mean PCE and core PCE - which you don't see in the trimmed-mean and core CPI series - comes down to a fundamental difference in how the Dallas Fed calculates the trimmed-mean PCE series: symmetric vs asymmetric trimming. The Cleveland Fed calculates its 16% trimmed-mean CPI symmetrically, i.e., it trims the bottom 8% and top 8% of the weighted monthly CPI price-change distribution. records.text: We expect the debate around AI disruption, and therefore uncertainty about many companies’ terminal value, will persist for at least several quarters. The threat of disruption will likely represent a persistent overhang until the later stages of AI adoption. In the meantime, disproving this disruption narrative is challenging. For investors to have confidence in the long-term impact of AI, it will require more evidence of where AI is impacting earnings, which could take several quarters if not years. We think more managements should prioritize discussions of the long-term outlook. The importance of terminal value underscores the importance of communicating long-term growth plans to investors. Multi-year guidance is inherently uncertain, but we believe a vision of addressable market size, growth, and profitability can influence investor perception of a company’s long-term growth prospects. Only 5% of S&P 500 companies discussed financial metrics beyond 5 years during their latest earnings calls, primarily within Utilities and Real Estate. Empirically, academic research has found evidence that a long-term orientation increases firm value and operating performance1. Similarly, the GS SUSTAIN team previously showed that companies with long-term incentive plans for managements typically outperform. 1 Caroline Flammer and Pratima Bansal, 2017. records.text: been our view that most n CEEMEA central banks could afford to wait and assess the duration and impact of the conflict, without the need to rush to tighten policy. This is due to three factors: (1) The inflationary backdrop was weak prior to the shock – aggregate demand was generally subdued, and inflation had surprised significantly to the downside in the months immediately before; (2) Policy rates were already above neutral prior to the conflict, making further tightening less likely; and (3) Exchange rates have remained relatively stable so far, reflecting high policy rates and healthy external balances. A notable exception is Türkiye, where growth and inflation were running high prior to the war and the Lira came under pressure, pushing the TCMB into action, though it kept policy unchanged last week. The longer the closure of the Strait persists and the higher energy prices climb, n the more this ‘wait and see’ approach is being challenged. With this set of revisions, we are adjusting our South Africa rate forecast to include two 25bp hikes in May and July (from on-hold previously) to a peak of 7.25%, which we expect to be unwound from 2027Q2 onwards, returning to a terminal rate of 5% (unchanged from earlier projections). We are not making other rate forecast changes at this time, but see the highest risk of hikes in Czechia and Ukraine. Bias toward asset swap spread tightening: We see risks skewed towards tightening under different scenarios in the Middle East conflict (which will remain a key driver of ASW). Worsening sentiment (i.e., re-escalation) would likely trigger a bigger sell-off in the swap curve than in the bond curve, echoing March’s sharp spread compression. With spreads already near pre-conflict levels, we see ample room to tighten should this scenario unfold. By contrast, a credible peace deal could initially push the spread wider as swaps rally faster than bonds, but the move could be limited. The market has largely stripped out the conflict-related risk premium (the 10y TIIE F is only 26bp above its pre-conflict level despite a >10% oil price surge), limiting a further rally and capping a widening of the spread. If the ceasefire does hold and the status quo persists, the spread still appears wide after recent local curve rallies. We expect the bond curve to gradually close the gap with the swap curve, helped by the strong peso that favors bonds and a likely consolidation of the swap curve given the lack of external meaningful developments. In the current circumstances, what differentiates an intermediate from a large deviation becomes consequential. Given the evidently exogenous and supply- driven nature of the current shock, if the mechanical deviation of headline inflation (between 3% and 4%) from target (2%) is deemed intermediate, then the correct response is to look through it. If it is deemed large, then none of the arguments we provided earlier stands any longer in the way of policy tightening. A generally hawkish Council, by which we mean a Council that puts substantial emphasis on the role of inflation expectations in the formation of prices, will hike regardless. The issue here is of course that what separates a large from an intermediate deviation of inflation from target is largely subjective. There is in our view no historically relevant data to calibrate this. Even the 2022 price shock remained, in our assessment, essentially a price shock. records.text: Global FX Strategy 27 April 2026 Citi Research 5 BoE Citi Econ Take: UK Economics and Rates – BoE: the case for holding Citi UK Economics is calling for no BoE hikes this year; rather, they expect the policy rate will remain on hold at 3.75%. Citi UK Rates expects Governor Bailey could once again push back on market pricing for hikes this year—as he did on 1 April. A 9–0 or an 8–1 vote split for no hike could further reinforce the MPC is likely to remain on hold for the foreseeable future. We have sympathy for this dovish potential, and relative central bank expectations are one of the factors causing us to forecast EURGBP higher over 2026 (other factors include UK political and fiscal risks, and positive fiscal impulse in the EU later in the year). In line with Econ and Rates views above, we see marginal dovish risk into the BoE meeting this week also given the weaker starting point for the UK pre-conflict (BoE was already being priced dovishly) and higher starting point for policy rates (e.g., more room to cut into neutral territory). On the margin, this could see a weaker GBP , but we also see limited market impact from guidance ahead of clarifying inflation data releases in the coming months (a BoE staying on hold in light of new higher inflation data would be a clearer, market-moving dovish signal, in our view). In that context, and given the Strait of Hormuz remains closed, there is some marginal hawkish risk for the ECB. In Europe, €CCC net downgrades were 8pp lower at 38%, while €B2s were 3pp lower from the February reading. Our fundamental models forecast that US defaults remain near current levels in the short-term, while EUR defaults can moderate further, albeit largely due to base effects. While the Iran conflict is increasing fundamental risks through higher commodity prices and potentially tighter global monetary policy, these risks are not likely to lead to higher 2026 default rates. Rather they present some upside risk for 2027 & 2028. We anticipate US spec-grade defaults to rise slightly from 4.1% today to 4.3% by YE'26 (Figure 7). There are still tighter financial conditions for B & CCC rated issuers, as AI disruptions produce outflows and downgrades within US BDCs and Leveraged Loans. However, low US recession risks and a Fed with the ability to ease policy if the economy weakens should offer a buffer to near-term defaults. European defaults will fall moderately from 3.7% to 2.7% by Q2'26, before reverting higher to 2.9% by YE'26 (Figure 8). There should be some base effects normalizing in the trailing 12-month default rate later this Spring as a number of May’25 defaults fall out of the look-back window. records.text: 2 Insights Information Classification: General SPOTLIGHT FX VIEWS Stay in high carry to ride Fed uncertainty. The April FOMC meeting highlighted a highly divided Committee, underscoring the complexity of the Fed’s policy tradeoffs rather than signaling a clear directional shift. This should not come as a surprise given that the Fed’s dual mandate is being tested by the growing stagflationary headwinds. The outcome reinforces the idea that US monetary policy is likely to remain uncertain and data -dependent, keeping rate volatility elevated even without an immediate policy move. In contrast, several EM central banks appear better positioned to withstand this US-driven volatility. Countries with high carry and a clearly hawkish bias offer stronger buffers against shifts in US rates. Brazil, South Africa, Turkey and post-election Hungary all fall into this category. Although long-end inflation expectations still have not converged to targets in those countries , credible hawkish central bank stances help maintain the attractive real yields and provide insulation against swings in US front-end and term-premium dynamics. BRL, TRY and HUF remain our favourite picks. Brazil stands out within this group. Twelve -month inflation expectations are still elevated at around 4.3%, above the 3% target, and real rates remain well above neutral (Figure 2). Accordingly, we now expect the Bank of Korea to deliver two 25bp rate hikes, with hikes being delivered in Q4 2026 and Q2 2027. On the timing of rate hikes, we acknowledge that the BoK could mull earlier rate hikes if we see strong signs of second round effects. New BoK Governor Hyun Song Shin recently said that it is not prudent to respond with monetary policy to a temporary shock. At the same time, he added that monetary policy response could be needed if the situation prolongs and leads to second round effects. In the scenario where core inflation rises faster than our current expectations, we think the BoK could consider rates hikes at an earlier timing. Having said that, our view remains that the BoK will patiently assess the Middle East conflict’s impact to its policy variables rather than rush to adjust policy rates. We still believe that the BoK will prefer a data-dependent approach rather than being pre-emptive, which is currently reflected in the pace and timing of our base case scenario. Specifically on second round effects, we think the rises on core inflation could be relatively modest compared to the high inflationary period during 2022-23. The changes we are making to our CEEMEA macro forecasts are less pronounced n than those made in the initial phases of the conflict (see here and here). There are two reasons for this: First, the changes to our commodities team’s price forecasts are smaller than those made earlier, with modest changes to oil price forecasts and no changes to gas price forecasts. Compared with Powell’s Fed which was more flexible and tolerant of inflation overshoots, Warsh would likely run a more rules-based, less reactive institution, with a smaller balance sheet and higher bar for intervention. Overall, he signals a shift away from more discretionary policy making, toward a more disciplined approach with a tighter definition of the Fed’s role. As we have discussed in prior research, every Fed Chair transition typically requires a learning period for the markets where they test the new chair's resolve and figure out how to interpret his/her communication style. This time should be no different, which could lead to some intermittent choppiness in the near-term caused by short spikes in bond volatility and/or stress in funding markets that are likely quite manageable.

Our prior projection would have argued for a significant change to Treasury’s guidance for auctions to remain unchanged for “at least the next several quarters,” but the later start date to coupon size increases leaves it slightly more of an open question. Although the Middle-East conflict may temporarily pause inflows into EM duration, we stay bullish over a multi-month horizon, expecting continued net purchases of local-currency EM bonds in the coming quarters as these securities take on a larger share of investors’ asset allocations (See Macro: EM–DM divide is fading). Within Latin America, Mexico currently stands out as the preferred destination thanks to a strong FX performance, modest fiscal concerns, and a relatively calm political environment (amid upcoming elections in Brazil and Colombia), implying that investors will likely demand a lower risk premium for Mbonos versus regional peers. We are entering a 2042 Mbonos vs 10 year TIIE F asset swap trade, viewing the risk as skewed toward a tightening of the spread after the recent widening. A potential increase in foreign ownership of Mbonos, on the back of a stable political environment, strong FX performance and modest fiscal pressures, would further supports the trade. Bias toward asset-swap spread tightening: We see risks skewed towards tightening under different Middle East conflict scenarios (Middle East conflict will remain a relevant driver of the ASW). Worsening sentiment (e.g., conflict resumption ) would likely trigger a sell off in the swap curve larger than in the bond curve, echoing March’s sharp compression of the spread. With spreads already near pre conflict levels, there’s ample room to tighten if this scenario unfolds.

However, a sizeable funding gap emerges in FY27 and beyond, as maturities are set to pick up, and both Treasury and TBAC have acknowledged that the next step will be increases sometime in FY27 (Figure 3). As a result, we see a significant risk that Treasury removes “at least” from the long-standing forward guidance that it “anticipates maintaining nominal coupon and FRN auction sizes for at least the next several quarters.” Beyond FY26, we expect Treasury to embark on a multi- quarter series of coupon increases beginning in February 2027 (Figure 4). Equities: US Leads the Pack Geopolitical events historically have not led to sustained volatility for US equities. Absent a sharp and persistent rise in oil prices (i.e., Brent>$100/bbl), we remain constructive on US markets due to the combination of positive operating leverage, supportive and pro-cyclical policy, and the potential for AI-driven efficiency gains. Beneficiaries of the Takaichi administration's reforms are likely to be more resilient. In EM, we find that low-volatility and high-dividend-yield stocks outperformed in prior geopolitical shocks while growth underperformed. While we shifted back to constructive EU equities at the start of this month, we anticipate a tactical pause to the rebound as the market awaits the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. What seems consistent, in contrast, is communication by Members of the Governing Council, which points to a very low level of patience, should the supply shock last a bit too long. This is of course the second input into the discussion on the direction of monetary policy. Combining those two marginal pieces of information makes us concede that the risk of rate hikes in the near term is a bit higher than we had in mind. Our change of “forecast” reflects that and no more than that. This in turn begs a number of questions: if the ECB hikes rate in a stagflationary environment, would it be a policy mistake? If so, may the Governing Council quickly have to reverse the hikes as it did in 2011? If it does not, why would it only hike twice? Etc. With the caveat again that policy has become immensely dependent on exogenous events, we try to answer those questions below by adopting a form of Socratic approach, and by considering in turn four horizons: (1) the very near-term, i.e. this week’s meeting of the Governing Council; (2) the next few months, covering the June and July meetings; (3) the latter part of the year (September to December); and (4) the medium-term, i.e. 2027 and beyond. This was best summarized by his question “why do we need to do that now?” Implicit in this framing were hints that the language could change in June. On the potential for rate hikes, Powell reiterated that “nobody is calling for a hike right now” but that, “if we need to hike, we will certainly signal that and we will certainly do it.” Amongst the factors that will determine any upcoming change in language and the direction and timing of the next move, Powell sounded relatively upbeat on economic fundamentals but cautious about the inflation outlook. On the former, Powell emphasized th at the labor market is showing “more and more signs of stability” and cited the current 4.3% unemployment rate as still low and near estimates of NAIRU. The resilient labor market is being supported by solid domestic demand growth (PDFP) , including “resilient” consumer spending, business fixed investment expanding at a “brisk pace” , and an “insatiable” demand for data centers. Many are contemplating the lagging impacts of higher commodity prices, similar to how investors were thinking through the effects of higher tariff rates a year ago. One of the single biggest methodological questions for the inflation market at the moment is how seriously we should take price signal from the commodity curves. All models are wrong, but some are useful The single biggest methodological question for the inflation market at the moment arguably is how seriously we should take the backwardation and forward price signal from the energy futures curves. This is crucial in thinking through the inflationary consequences of the war in Iran, which will first-order, but not exclusively, come through the energy commodities channel. Unsurprisingly, there has been a rather tight historical relationship between realized crude oil prices and the CPI energy commodities index, so forecasters and markets pay close attention the signal from the Brent, WTI and/or RBOB curves (among others) ( Figure 1). BoE Recap—Keeping Options Open The MPC voted 8-1 to hold Bank Rate at the April meeting, with Pill dissenting in favour of a 25bp hike. The vote split was in line with consensus expectations, although we had expected that Greene would also support raising Bank Rate at this meeting. The Monetary Policy Summary noted a “risk of material second-round effects” that policy “would need to lean against”. At the same time, it also acknowledged that a weakening economy and tightening financial conditions could help to moderate inflationary pressures. The Summary noted that the MPC judged a hold to be appropriate “at this meeting” while reiterating that the Committee “stands ready to act as necessary” to keep inflation on course to meet the target. The Bank showed three scenarios for the economic outlook in the MPR, varying the assumptions on energy prices as well as the extent of second-round effects. T-bill supply ramps up in Q3 Source: US Treasury, Barclays Research Beyond the near term, we think the Treasury is unlikely to increase coupon auction sizes this year, and so expect net T-bill issuance to private investors at around $450bn. That said, we believe coupon auction size increases are approaching – as discussed in our recent update on deficits (see US Fiscal Outlook: Supply pays the bill) – because absent higher coupons, T-bill needs would continue to grow, eventually putting strain on the market. For instance, in a scenario where Treasury holds coupon auction sizes unchanged through 2027, net T-bill issuance to investors would be on the order of $615bn (assuming ongoing Fed RMPs of $20bn per month in 2027). While higher than the recent run rate, this would not be especially alarming. However, looking ahead to 2028, net T-bill issuance would rise to around $1trn absent coupon increases, which would be materially more challenging for the bill market to absorb. The Treasury will also need to consider risks to T-bill demand, particularly from the Fed, as it evaluates options for balance sheet reduction that could materialize under a Warsh-led Fed. We expect hikes in June and July with risks of delay/less Given our expectation of higher energy prices persisting through the year, we continue to expect hikes in June and July (with risks of one) as an insurance to guard against second round effects. We then expect three quarterly cuts from Q2 2027 to 3.5%, with risks of 3.25%. Risks of delays on hikes have increased after today’s lack of explicit guidance on June. But we think if higher inflation expectations are sustained, energy prices stay elevated and growth/labour market doesn’t worsen materially, then the BoE would need to lean against risks of second round effects as soon as June. The longer it waits the greater the risks that higher inflation persists for longer. We do think the bar for more than 50bps of hikes is high. At the same time if by mid-year, the shock subsides and it looks like energy prices are moving lower, the labour market/economy worsens materially or inflation/wage expectations fall, then chances will rise that the BoE looks through the shock and keeps rates on hold through 2026, with cuts in 2027. Rates: waiting – the only game in town Current market pricing for 2026 looks broadly consistent with our read of today’s meeting: a June hike is possible but now looks slightly less certain than we had assumed pre-meeting; the evolution of forward-looking data should guide the BoE’s next steps, and comparison of our outlook with the BoE’s scenario analysis still points to one to two hikes in 2026. Thailand has been facing pressure from rising structural deficits. With an enlarging government, falling revenue to GDP ratio, rising interest share of the budget, and the need for the fiscal sector to absorb frequent economic shocks, debt consolidation is a challenge without ambitious government spending and revenue reforms. If the government cannot increase the tax base or introduce new taxes, a tax increase may prove inevitable. The Mathematics of Sustainability (r–g) The fundamental vulnerability of the Thai fiscal position is the narrowing spread between the nominal interest rate (r) and the nominal GDP growth rate (g). The debt sustainability equation, Δd = (r − g)d + pb, dictates that when borrowing costs exceed growth, the debt ratio rises automatically, even without new spending. At current debt levels (~67% of GDP), every 1% of positive r-g spread adds 0.67 percentage points to the debt ratio annually. Currently, Thailand’s r-g is close to zero, meaning structural deficits do not need to worsen for debt to drift higher; the mathematics work against consolidation on its own. Consequently, raising the growth path (g) is no longer a development aspiration but a mechanical fiscal necessity to prevent self-reinforcing debt accumulation. Further, Brazil will launch a programme to help people in debt, which can promote a cumulative stimulus impulse in a still very resilient economy, we argue, complicating the monetary-policy path. Oil shock meets political pressure The Middle East conflict has sent international oil prices soaring, reopening the domestic energy price gap that Brazil has navigated repeatedly over the past decade. With Brent prices rising sharply, domestic fuel prices now sit about 70% below international reference levels for gasoline and roughly 50% below for diesel. Against this backdrop, the Lula administration has moved quickly on multiple fronts, combining tax relief, producer subsidies, energy export tariff adjustments and an agenda to reduce household debt. The government is now aiming for a major social welfare state reform, especially since rising non-wage labour costs are increasingly burdening the corporate sector. Reform options include a gradual increase in the retirement age to up to 70 years or linking the retirement age to the years of service, eliminating costly early retirement programs and the reintroduction of the so-called sustainability factor (which automatically dampens pension increases when there are fewer contributors). Timeline and likelihood of success. The pension commission is tasked with developing proposals by the end of June. As the third element of a wider reform package (see health care, income tax as discussed above), we expect both coalition partners to eventually agree on reforming the statutory pension system. Linking the retirement age to years of contributions (if not to the increasing life expectancy directly) would contribute to stabilizing the system. records.text: The near-term directions of both market breadth and momentum will depend on the macroeconomic outlook and the read-through from the Q1 earnings season. An improvement in the geopolitical outlook would likely broaden both earnings revisions and market performance, helping recent laggards like consumer stocks rebound in a “catch up.” Conversely, a severe deterioration in the war that raises concerns about semiconductor supply chains or causes investors to reduce their equity market exposures would likely catalyze a “catch down.” Earnings season results and commentary could also shift the market’s perception of the outlook for AI-related spending and earnings, affecting the recent market leaders. However, mega-cap hyperscaler results this week catalyzed a further increase in consensus capex estimates and will likely extend recent market momentum. Over the medium term, market breadth is unlikely to fully normalize without a maturation of the AI trade. Eventually, clarity regarding the widespread impact of AI should expand the AI trade to include “winners” outside of the infrastructure complex, including companies boosting revenues by selling AI products and companies using AI to increase productivity. Electoral reform: no longer a given One area that appears to confirm the government’s weakened position is electoral reform. As previously highlighted, reform of the electoral law had been in the pipeline, with the stated aim of improving governability through a system delivering clearer majorities. With general elections expected in the second quarter of 2027, the informal convention is that any new electoral law should be approved by the autumn (6 months before). Ahead of the March constitutional referendum, we had flagged the possibility of accelerated (by summer) approval of the new electoral law in the event of a “Yes” victory. After the vote, we expected a slower timetable for reform. However, what emerged from our discussions in Rome is that the reform itself now looks far less certain. While the electoral law can technically be changed by a simple parliamentary majority – being an ordinary law – the ruling coalition no longer appears united around the need for reform. The main issue is declining conviction in the political convenience of changing the electoral system, a reassessment that also reflects current opinion polls. Meanwhile, our positioning proxy indicates that mutual funds moved close to neutral duration versus their benchmarks, while macro/CTA funds also remained broadly neutral. H.8 data show that banks' securities holdings rose over the week to April 15, with roughly $11bn in MBS and $8bn in USTs. The increase in MBS was driven primarily by large domestic banks, while that in USTs was led by foreign banks, which added about $4bn. Valuation effects appear to have contributed a small part of the increase, as rates edged slightly lower over the week. Year to date, bank securities holdings are $141bn higher, including $78bn in USTs, extending the sector's solid demand for securities in 2025. Meanwhile, deposits fell by $32bn, and we expect the next H.8 release to show a larger drop, as has typically been the case around the tax deadline ($200bn in 2025 and $256bn in 2024, for example). On the foreign side, Japanese investor demand was broadly flat in the week to April 17, an improvement compared with the prior four-week average, at $5bn in net foreign note and bond sales. Given our view that the current shock is stagflationary, which means that it will result in a marked erosion of demand in coming quarters, we struggle with the idea that the Governing Council continues to hike rates when this becomes evident. That is why we assume as a “baseline” only two hikes, with risks if anything slightly to the downside. That raises then the question of whether the Governing Council can reverse any hike, as happened in 2011. Nothing strikes us as impossible in the current environment, but we currently see the probability of such a course of action as fairly low. Just as we see the current situation as every different from 2022, we also see it as very different from 2011: First, in 2011, the ECB hiked policy rates at a time when the self-imposed recession that would eventually compel it to cut rates again was already unfolding. The economy was entering a credit crunch, caused by an effective downgrading of all unsecured bank debt, itself the consequence of the migration of sovereign credit from safe to risky in 2010, and then of the uncertainty about the outcome of the bank stress tests in the summer of 2011. On each given day, we blend data by adding the total quoted amount in the order book from both sources for each displayed currency pair. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. For example, a 90th percentile reading for EURUSD indicates that the current depth of book value is ranked in the top 10% of historical observations over the last year. Volume data from July 2020 onwards represents the combined total traded volume across EBS and Reuters sources. Prior to July 2020, we aggregate total traded volume from EBS with estimated trading volume from Reuters, which is calculated as a product of total paid-given count and average trade size. To estimate average trade size prior to July 2020 we use all future data for total trading volume and trade count. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. Spread data represents the average daily market spread based on quotes taken every 30 seconds in the order book aggregated across EBS and Reuters on a volume weighted basis. records.text: Cayla Seder April 30, 2026 1 Insights Classification: Premium Material D M Inf lation In Focu s : Hot to th e touch, but not the core INFLATION TRENDS. It is a surprise to no one that inflation remains eye‑wateringly hot. That said, there is far more to glean than the headline alone: the direction of travel and breadth of inflation matter most for assessing how price pressures transmit into policy—and ultimately asset valuations. On the surface, DM inflation in April was abnormally strong, rising an average of 84bp m/m. However, this marked a moderation from March’s 121bp surge. Importantly, April’s print was driven by a less forceful increase in energy pr ices. DM fuel prices rose 9.79% m/m on average, down from 17.63% in March —still extreme by historical standards, but an improvement nonetheless. This also indicates that at this stage, energy-led inflation is not meaningfully feeding into other facets of the economy. For example, food inflation through April 24 th rose just 23bp m/m on average, a stark contrast . This benign backdrop is clearly fragile: while a ceasefire is in place, the Strait remains closed, removing more roughly 10% of global oil supply. B rent has returned to triple‑digit territory, and the longer the disruption persists, the greater the risk that fuel inflation bleeds into broader price dynamics. They will need to discuss the longer timeline of the conflict and how they will factor in surging energy prices into their intermediate term models. Markets have already spoken on this front, tightening current year and future rate views by up to 70 bps. Current market pricing for 2026 looks broadly consistent with our read of today’s meeting: a June hike is possible but now looks slightly less certain than we had assumed pre-meeting; the evolution of forward-looking data should guide the BoE’s next steps, and comparison of our macroeconomic outlook with the BoE’s scenario analysis still points to one to two hikes in 2026. Geopolitical sentiment has been the key driver of oil prices, which has fed through directly into higher outright yields, curve flattening, EGB spread widening, tenor basis tightening and higher implied rates vol. That the Middle East conflict remains the key factor for rates price action near term is not in question. However, it is worth flagging that the reactivity of implied rates vol to oil appears to have declined. For example, as Figure 1 shows, the beta of 1y10y implied rates volatility to oil prices has fallen in recent weeks. The inflation outlook is arguably as cloudy as it was at the time of the March meeting. Although equities are trading as though the Iran war is over, gas is still above $4 and traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is still highly disrupted. As a result, uncertainty about the impact of the conflict on core inflation remains elevated. Meanwhile, the recent labor data (March jobs, ADP, claims) show resilience and potentially some green. records.text: Second part of report titleUS copper imports surge in 2026 on tariff fears: In 2025, US net copper imports jumped by 216% to 988kt (1.78Mt of imports and 789kt of exports). We believe much of this increase went into visible CME inventory, which jumped by 367kt last year, with a further 450–500kt going into non-visible inventory. Many commentators had expected this draw of metal into the US to prompt extreme tightness in the LME market and the onshore Chinese market, with some suggesting China would run out of copper inventory, but these fears never materialised. Indeed, while US net imports have been slowing over the first two months of 2026, inventory actually built rapidly in LME and SHFE warehouses. Copper import tariffs may not materialise: Just as the Trump administration decided against refined copper tariffs on 30 July last year after intense consumer industry lobbying, and against tariffs on critical minerals such as silver in a decision made on 14 January this year, we think the same will occur for the upcoming 26 June deadline for the next copper tariff decision. The weight of metal now sitting in the US has driven CME copper to trade at discounts to LME copper since the start of January this year, reducing the incentive to move more metal into the US. We expect a sustained downtrend in US imports through 2026. Weight of metal on and off exchange in the US has crushed the CME premium over LME Sources: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas Sources: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas US: Copper

Page 3 Generally, these measures have similar monthly prints, deviating only when there are particularly large increases in certain core components that get stripped out by trimmed-mean and median. For example, the large run up in used car prices in 2021 boosted core CPI and PCE but was omitted by the alternative inflation measures. Similarly, recent core PCE prints have been elevated by large increases in small goods categories like software and computer accessories that trimmed- mean and median are “looking through”. In year-over-year terms (Figures 3 and 4), median measures seems to run higher than core or trimmed -mean for both CPI and PCE , at least post -GFC and pre - covid. For the CPI , trimmed-mean was relatively in line with core, likel y because the trim amount is relatively small and is more likely to capture the volatile food and energy categories relative to other goods and services. In contrast, trimmed- mean PCE cuts more of the distribution. As such, it has been more likely to diverge from core and has tended to run at or slightly above core over this period. Are trimmed-mean measures better? Is there necessarily a clear reason to focus on trimmed-mean measures of inflation when setting monetary policy? records.text: A closer look at AI-related debt supply Similar to the increased fluidity across the private credit and syndicated leveraged loan markets, AI-related data center financing provides an example of a similar convergence between the traditional IG and HY bond markets and more novel structures. For example, bond issuance representing joint venture (JV) deals for specific data center build-outs have grown to nearly $76 billion of the broader $400 billion of AI-related gross issuance across USD IG and HY since 2H2025 (Exhibit 1). Generally speaking, the issuer of the bonds is an entity building a data center which has been pre-leased to a tenant. In most cases, the tenant is an AI-cloud platform or subsidiary of a hyperscaler. In either scenario, the (typically highly-rated) hyperscaler provides a backstop on long-term lease obligations through support and lease recognition agreements. In some instances, the bonds include structural protections such as mandatory debt amortization and defined cash flow management through a ‘lockbox’ feature. Some bonds are fully amortizing, while others are structured to leave a portion of the principal outstanding, which will require refinancing at a later date. Many indentures allow for the issuance of additional debt if certain criteria are met. In the event of a payment default or bankruptcy by the lessee, the hyperscaler has an obligation to assume the lease or pay a termination fee. records.text: 27 April 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 9 5) Reform of the debt brake - still mission impossible The starting point. On September 11, an expert commission started to discuss how to modernize the debt brake beyond the three key reforms that have been agreed on at the end of March 2025. To recall, this had been unlimited spending for defence beyond 1% of GDP, the establishment of a EUR 500 bn off-budget fund for infrastructure and climate, and the provision for German states to run annual structural primary deficits of 0.35% of GDP. Reform options. The expert commission is now tasked with developing proposals on how to modernize the debt brake. Recent research papers suggest introducing flexible thresholds for net credit borrowing depending on the debt level (see Bundesbank and Council of Economic Advisors ) and/or aligning national fiscal rules with EU fiscal rules by moving from static thresholds to debt sustainability analysis and expenditure paths (see here). Timeline and likelihood of success . The debt brake commission is expected to meet again by the end of May with discussion apparently deadlocked at the moment.6 For the CDU, debt brake reform is not something they want to accelerate and they frame it as "minor technical details"7 that have to be clarified. Contrary to the Social Democrats, they do not see the reform resulting in more fiscal leeway than the March 2025 reform allowed. Overall, we do not expect quick progress on more substantial renewed reforms.

In this piece, we give background on such alternative gauges and explore if they are in fact superior to more traditional headline and core measures. ▪ We find that in a low and stable inflation environment, focusing on the trimmed-mean may have some advantages . However , it may systematically ignore inflation rates in the tails of the cross -sectional distribution that could be useful in identifying turning points and transitions to more volatile inflation regimes. ▪ As an example , trimmed-mean rose slower than headline or core post - covid, taking about six months longer to rise above 3% in 2021.
