records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 1 Next 12-Months Outlook: Our High-Conviction Calls Deciphering Economic Momentum: Energy disruptions are starting to impact global economies - we model the impact to the supply side of the economy to a one quarter shock. There is a difference between a physical oil disruption and a price shock - a key difference, particularly in Asia and Europe where exposure varies dramatically between volume risks and price risks because in Asia, price risk is often alleviated by fiscal support to smooth price volatility. Duration is key; if oil prices were to stay above $100, we would expect central banks raise to concerns about inflation risks. The downside risks to growth become more material if the high oil prices last longer or rise towards the demand destruction level above $125 for a period of time. Staying Close to Home: Lingering uncertainty around oil supply disruption means outcomes for risk assets are less balanced - either we return to pre-March backdrop if tanker flows resume quickly, or markets sell off in earnest as recession probability rises on Brent spiking. We are EW global equities, UW fixed income, OW cash, with the biggest UW in corporate credit on binary spread outcomes. We continue to like US in stocks and government bonds given the region's better fundamentals, more defensive nature versus other regions. records.text: US equity market breadth has narrowed in recent weeks to one of its lowest levels on record. The S&P 500 has rallied by 14% from its low in late March and now trades at a new record high. However, the median S&P 500 constituent remains 13% below its respective high. That divergence has lowered our preferred measure of S&P 500 market breadth to its lowest level since the Dot-Com Bubble outside of briefly in mid-2023. The narrow breadth rally has been driven primarily by stocks tied to the AI infrastructure build-out, mirroring the narrow breadth of recent earnings revisions. The SOX Semiconductor Index has jumped by 30% since the start of the Iran War and the Magnificent 7 have collectively risen by 10%, while the equal-weight S&P 500 has declined by 1% over that period. The narrowness of the market rally has reflected the narrowness of recent S&P 500 earnings estimate upgrades, which have also been concentrated in Technology stocks. records.text: 27 April 2026 Focus Germany Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Klingbeil's "Schröder moment"? - a speech that kickstarted structural reforms Back in the 2000s, an SPD-led government pushed through far-reaching labour market and welfare reforms. A recent speech by FinMin Klingbeil raised hopes that this reform spirit could be recaptured now. He outlined a reform agenda that aims to increase work incentives, curb non-wage labour costs and link the retirement age to the years of service. New reform momentum might affect sentiment positively at a crucial juncture, when the energy-price spike has become more than a speed bump in Germany’s road to recovery, leading to us downgrading our growth forecast to 0.5% this year (see here). All three parties are now staking out their negotiating positions. This also involves making maximum demands, like the SPD on a higher inheritance tax, the CSU on cutting subsidies/ raising commuter allowance and the CDU on raising the statutory pension age. During upcoming negotiations, a compromise within the negotiating space sketched out in the table below is likely to be reached. We expect the reform process to be multi-staged with legislative proposals for health care reform by the end of April, for income tax reform by the end of May, and a pension reform proposal by the end of June, with first concrete legislative proposals by October at the earliest. records.text: Market outlook of life insurers Regarding the median market outlook for H1 FY26, the range for 10y JGB yields was 2.05-2.95%, with a year-end value of 2.45%. Compared to the previous survey in October (range: 1.40–2.00%, year-end: 1.75%), the range has shifted higher against a backdrop of expectations for a high- pressure economy under the Takaichi administration since last autumn and rising inflation uncertainty since March amid heightened Middle East tensions: the lower bound has risen by 65bp, the median by 70bp and the upper bound by 95bp. In other words, while the median implies limited upward pressure on yields from current levels, the high degree of uncertainty persists (Figure 6). Among the companies that provided forecasts for superlong JGB yields, the range for the FY-end 20y JGB yield was 3.00–3.70%, with the lower bound up 70bp and the upper bound up 65bp from the previous survey in October. The 30y yield range also shifted upward, with the lower bound at 3.3% (previously 2.8%) and the upper bound at 4.2% (previously 3.5%). The range for the 10y UST yield forecast was 3.50–4.68%, with a year-end value of 4.15%. Compared to the previous survey (3.50-4.60%, 4.00%), the range’s upper bound and the end- period level were revised up by 8bp and 15bp, respectively, but remain broadly within the range for 10y UST yields seen over the past year. records.text: Foreign official demand: Custody confusion Separately, custody holdings at the NY Fed, widely seen as a timely proxy for foreign official demand, have fallen sharply over the past year. This has raised concerns about foreign appetite for USTs. TIC data, on other hand, show that foreign officials have net bought Treasuries over the same period ( Figure 9). In our recent report (see here), we discuss the reasons for the discrepancy, highlighting that the Fed custody data only includes foreign central banks (and some other international organizations) that keep Treasuries in Fed custody. TIC data coverage is broader as it includes Treasuries held by private custodians too. TIC data also suggest that the official sector is more diverse than is commonly perceived. On the one hand, it shows a recent shift in duration preference, with more appetite for shorter-duration Treasuries, including T-bills. On the other, it also shows a growing appetite for corporate bonds and equities. That said, Fed custody holdings of USTs fell sharply in March, which might very well reflect official net sales, given the decline in FX reserves for some countries. We await the March TIC data, to be released on May 18, to assess to what extent aggregate foreign official demand fell. FIGURE 9. records.text: M Idea 2 Interest Rate Strategy United States | When the not surprising surprises anyway MORGAN STANLEY & CO. LLC Matthew Hornbach, CMT Matthew.Hornbach@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-1863 Aryaman Singh Aryaman@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-1993 Martin Tobias, CFA, CMT Martin.Tobias@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-6076 Shaun Zhou Shaun.Zhou@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-6076 Eli Carter Eli.Carter@morganstanley.com +1 212 761-4703 Remember the weather in March Last week began with two robust data points: the ADP weekly employment data showed the economy created ~55k jobs, on average, in the 4 weeks ending April 4. That period - spanning from March 8 through April 4 - included the week of March 12, the same day to which the March nonfarm payroll report anchors its data. Given the large upside surprise in the March payroll report, which included a boost from weather according to our economics team, the improvement in the ADP weekly series should not come as a surprise. Remember, the San Francisco Fed estimated that weather added roughly ~240k jobs to the March report. In addition, remember the week-to-week volatility in the weekly ADP series over the past 12 months exceeds most of the post-pandemic period and handily exceeds the pre- pandemic period. In other words, treat the weekly ADP series with extreme caution. records.text: 1 Insights Classification: ComplimentaryMaterial FOMC Preview: Hawks flying higher April 27, 2026 Policy stasis: The Fed will remain on hold this week, as the case for policy statis has only gotten stronger since the start of the war. And while the Committee’s median view of policy patience before the war came with wide bands of opinions, surging prices since the energy shock may make for strange bedfellows. This has been evident in recent Fed speak, which at best has been less dovish and at worst, can be interpreted as hawkish. Included in these statements, were views shared by Daly, who raised the prospect that keeping rate unchanged this year could successfully restrain inflation without jeopardizing the jobs market. Waller who had dovishly leaned into labour weakness cited upside risk to inflation from both the war and the labour markets. And even Miran, the most dovish member has been less so recently, adjusting his call for 4-cuts down to 3 going into the last FOMC meeting. Our media readings (Figure 1) of members and the Fed shows this shift, with even the most dovish voters trending hawkishly, while the reading for the overall institution is now near neutral. We therefore expect the Fed to sound hawkish in the face of uncertainty. This is largely expected by the markets, which have pushed the next rate cut into late 2027, which signals a growing view that the current cutting cycle is over. The implications are twofold, in our view. First, AI has likely put a relative floor under the back-end of spread curves for associated capital structures where traditional supply and demand dynamics no longer fully capture what is a higher term premium. If that is right, further issuance will likely take curves steeper than anticipated. Second, M&A and broader long-end corporate issuance may prove to be the better barometer for curve direction from here. Primary supply tenor, which has a cleaner pass-through to curve shape for Non-Tech capital structures, should continue to skew longer, as corporate activity has notably remained robust and the funding mix for M&A skews credit negative. One key risk to this view is a prolonged commodity market disruption, which could steepen the back end of rates curves while also creating bear-flattening pressure on spread curves if investors mark down growth expectations. Beyond the obvious volatility of the environment, the answer to this question ought to be found in the reason for which the ECB hiked in the first place. If it is because of a fear of non-linearities in price formation, then it is reasonable to think that the intent of the ECB is (1) to assert credibility and (2) to rein in demand to bring prices down faster. An “insurance” hike of merely 25 bps seems to make little sense in this context. We do not see the typical curve-flattening pressures that often accompany acute Italian credit concerns and BTP spreads have been resilient relative to implied volatility, rate levels and broader EUR equity performance. Moreover, part of the recent volatility in BTPs reflects their role as a liquid proxy for risk, with the IK future frequently used by investors as a hedging instrument when alternatives are less accessible. Our positioning indicators also suggest that sentiment toward Italy has held up relatively well. In futures, investor positioning remains net long, and relative to Bunds has stayed net long even through the Middle East escalations. In our FXRS survey, the duration positioning in euro area peripherals has moderated but is still in overweight territory. Repo signals point to a rise in BTP short interest since March, though not to levels comparable with the 2022-23 period ( European Rates Watch: EGB supply, positioning & flows 17 April 2026). That said, as we have revised down our growth expectations lower (0.2% in 2026, and 0.6% in 2027) we are increasingly concerned that the market may suddenly question the certainty of Italian debt-sustainability. In that context, we see the outlook for BTP–Bund spreads as increasingly binary and remain cautious at current levels. Meanwhile, USD funding via medium- to long-term currency swaps related to credit assets, together with USD funding related to the US-Japan investment deal (see FX & xccy insights: US-Japan investment deal and market implications, Vol. 4, dated 23 March), is likely to put widening pressure on the medium- to long-term USDJPY xccy basis. In fact, we estimate that currency-swap funding related to the US-Japan investment deal amounts to JPY25-36trn, which would correspond to one-third to one-half of the existing currency swaps outstanding (about JPY73trn; Figure 9) held by Japanese institutional investors such as banks and life insurers, suggesting significant widening pressures on xccy basis. We continue to recommend 1y1y/5y5y USDJPY xccy basis flattener trade. With USDJPY staying elevated near intervention- concern levels, appetite for FX-unhedged foreign bond investment is generally limited here, but in phases where the market heads toward the range’s lower bound or the low-to-mid 150s implied by the end-period forecast, some bottom-fishing demand could be triggered, potentially becoming a factor that somewhat restrains JPY appreciation. 27 April 2026 3 Barclays | Japan Flow Update

We think that a more prolonged restrictive rate environment, coupled with wider spreads across key sectors at risk of disruption due to AI, could weigh heavily on the lowest quality pockets of loan markets. Front-end IG screens attractive Despite the overall rates-spread correlation remaining negative at an index level, sensitivities have differed across IG tenors. Since the start of March, average rolling monthly correlations have shifted most aggressively and flipped to positive in front-end IG (1-3y) but have remained negative further out the curve. As a result, the US IG term structure has flattened, both in yield terms and in spread terms, and US IG 1-3y is starting to look cheap versus the belly. Despite higher realized vol in front-end spreads, our latest Carry Model update also favors front-end positioning and the US IG 1–3y point specifically, where spreads have lagged the broader rally. Conversely, in a risk-off event or if markets begin to price a growth shock, we think yield curves could bull steepen as the Fed turns more dovish, which would also benefit front-end yields more than the belly, duration aside. With this in mind, we open a new trade: Long US IG 1-3y vs. Short US IG 3-5y (duration matched 2:1).

BoJ Citi Econ Take: BoJ Preview – Expecting hawkish hold, voting behavior again in focus The long-held base case of Citi Economics has been a rate hike once every six months, with the next hike coming in July. The two most recent public appearances by Governor Ueda offered no clear signal for an imminent rate hike, and market pricing for a hike has fallen sharply. That said, even if the policy rate is unchanged at this meeting, the hold is likely to be hawkish given concerns about further JPY depreciation and the risk of falling behind the curve. We will be closely watching the voting behavior of board members to gauge the degree of hawkishness. At the March meeting, the number of dissenting votes did not increase, which we interpreted as a signal that the BoJ intends to maintain its wait-and-see stance. An increase in the number of dissenting votes increase at this meeting could be interpreted as the BoJ laying the groundwork for a rate hike in the near future. Notably, despite recent USD weakness during the deescalation phase of the US- Iran conflict, USDJPY has remained elevated and EURJPY has climbed to a new all- time high. If the BoJ leaves its policy unchanged at this week’s meeting, USDJPY could well climb past 160. In this case, we think the Japanese government would likely intervene to buy the JPY and try to push USDJPY back to around 155. records.text: e experience of 2022 is more likely than we thought to hike rates if the ongoing negative supply shock persists. We have therefore included two 25 bp hikes in our model expectation. Latter part of the year: recognising the erosion of demand — Our basic take on the current shock is that higher prices do not result from excess demand, but will on the contrary rapidly cause an erosion of demand, especially for discretionary items. That erosion of demand ought to convince the ECB not to follow through with more policy tightening. 2027 and beyond: shift in the policy mix — While we think rate hikes now would likely be unnecessary, we would not expect them to be reversed because our expectation of rapidly rising pressure for fiscal spending on defence, energy, technology, etc suggests a gradual move to a policy mix that includes more expansionary fiscal policy, and generally tighter monetary policy. Appendix There are various methods to estimate the share of present value represented by the “terminal value” of an equity. The GS dividend discount model (“DDM”) is based on modeled earnings and dividends. We modify our DDM to account for the growing use of buybacks as a form of returning cash to shareholders. We modestly scale down realized buybacks to account for their relative variability versus dividends. However, a dividend discount model is challenging for companies that do not pay a dividend, such as some high growth companies. We introduce a discounted cash flow model (“DCF”) in this report, which is based on modeled sales growth, margins, capex, and depreciation. Like the DDM, the DCF uses a 10-year forecast horizon. Exhibit 12 shows the estimated share of S&P 500 value in the terminal value over time for both approaches, which are broadly similar. records.text: Second part of report title 27/04/2026 3 Middle East conflict scenarios PRICE SCENARIOS David Wilson, Head of Metals Strategy | BNP Paribas Singapore Branch Sources: Bloomberg, BNP Paribas We think the short-term outlook for copper prices is highly dependent on events in the Middle East. We look at how our oil scenarios published in Energy: Potential for de-escalation but upside risks remain on 9 April filter through to copper. De-escalation: Should rapid progress to a sustainable ceasefire occur and oil prices fall to a floor of USD80/bbl, we would expect a sharp speculative jump in copper prices, potentially to USD15,000/t. However, we believe such spikes would drive significant end-user buying resistance and ultimately dramatically exacerbate already-evident demand destruction. This, in our view, would drive a sharp price correction H2-25, like the one seen in May–September 2024 following copper’s first speculative push to over USD11,000/t. Ceasefire doesn’t hold but de-escalation in Q2: In this scenario, we still see copper initially rallying on ceasefire optimism, but ceasefire failure means sustained higher oil prices (at about USD140/bbl) while parties continue to negotiate, leading to a stronger USD and slower global demand growth. We see this as effectively our copper base case. Over the past week, funding markets continued to show minimal signs of pressure even as the TGA hovered around the $1trn mark. The continued lack of strain through month-end has reinforced our view that funding conditions in May are likely to be very soft. We estimate the TGA will fall to around $900bn on May 1 and then to about $800bn by mid-month, an average level $830bn for the month( Figure 1). This would leave reserves meaningfully above current levels, even as SOFR printed below the effective funds rate yesterday. In that environment, it is conceivable that SOFR will average below the funds rate in May, given the $200bn+ increase in reserves that we are expecting from the highs in the TGA. records.text: M Idea 8 The remaining scenario involves a Democratic win of both chambers where the party is able to build a clear consensus around a political agenda. While the President retains veto power in this outcome, the Democrats could extract concessions (see above). Perhaps more importantly for markets, investors may then look ahead to 2028 in this outcome with the assumption that the odds of a Democrat sweep (including the Presidency) appear likely to rise. This could lead the market to question the durability of the current policy path – specifically, de-regulation (which aids the Banks and small/mid caps), the full scope of the One Big Beautiful Bill (which has helped Industrials and Technology), and the rebalancing from government to the private sector that we have been focused on (see here and here). In our view, this could lead to an initial risk-off reaction function either before mid-terms if polling/prediction markets convincingly point in this direction or post midterms. Why not a more sustained risk-off move? The President has veto power and the 2028 Presidential election would still be 2 years away. In terms of the historical performance precedent in midterm election years, defensives have typically outperformed in the months leading up to midterms with broad markets gaining 10% in 1Q but giving back half of these returns during Q2 and Q3 before bottoming at the start of Q4. Relative leadership during this period comes from Health Care, Staples, Utilities, and Telecom.

records.Author: BofA Euro Economics; Chiara Angeloni; Edvard Davidsson; Ruben Segura-Cayuela
records.text: 2 Euro Area Watch | 27 April 2026 Macro Chiara Angeloni BofA Europe (Milan) chiara.angeloni@bofa.com Ruben Segura -Cayuela BofA Europe (Madrid) ruben.segura-cayuela@bofa.com Macro: more fragile scenario Our field trip proved to be exceptionally timely, as during the very hours we were in Rome the Italian Minister of Economy and Finance released the updated fiscal document (DFP 2026) with revised macroeconomic projections. In the Treasury’s updated estimates, GDP growth has been revised down to 0.6% for this year (10bps lower than previously projected). Growth is also forecast at 0.6% in 2027 and 0.8% in 2028-29. The 2026 growth profile still appears optimistic to us, although we acknowledge the unusually high uncertainty surrounding any baseline scenario. records.text: The value of “terminal value” The risk from AI disruption has intensified debate about the “terminal value” of equities. Software has been at the epicenter of this debate. Share prices of a group of software stocks are down 19% YTD, but selling pressure has spread to other asset-light industries. For these stocks, which have much of their value concentrated in the distant future, large recent price declines contrast with resilient near-term earnings, underscoring the importance of the long-term growth outlook. Using a 10-year modified dividend discount model, we estimate that the terminal value represents roughly 75% of S&P 500 equity value today, near the highest level in 25 years. We estimate the present value of earnings, dividends, and net buybacks for 10 years and assume the remainder of equity value is in the “terminal value” (see Appendix for details). The majority of the equity value is in the terminal value by design, as it represents the value not a ccounted for by the finite 10-year horizon chosen for the dividend discount model (“DDM”). However, today’s share of value in the terminal value is elevated versus history and mirrors other periods where investor long-term growth expectations were increasingly optimistic, including the Dot Com Boom. In addition, while hedge fund gross leverage has declined during the last couple weeks, it remains elevated relative to history, ranking at the upper end of the 5-year range for both the overall hedge fund universe and fundamental equity long/short funds specifically. At the index level, sharply narrowing market breadth signals drawdown risk, and elevated current positioning exacerbates that risk. Sharp declines in market breadth have historically preceded larger-than-average S&P 500 drawdowns in the subsequent 6-12 months. The elevated current level of our US Equity Sentiment Indicator of investor positioning has also been a signal for below-average near-term S&P 500 returns in the past. However, the positioning indicator remains far below previous highs, and the tool is a stronger statistical indicator at low levels than at high levels. The obvious variables are the construction timeline and access to power infrastructure, but more traditional project finance questions also matter. Responsibilities and remedies for cost overruns are important risk factors. Investors prefer guaranteed maximum cost prices (GMPs), reliable construction companies, and overrun risk to be borne by tenants, not landlords. IG-rated bonds typically have either no construction risk or some combination of GMPs in place and/or overrun costs directly passing through to the tenant. Leases in many HY bonds include delay thresholds after which the tenant is either allowed to terminate the lease, be compensated with lease credits, or other remedies. Typically, overrun clauses span 180 days but can vary and are one of the clearest conduits for construction risk. Coverage: As with any lease-backed structure, debt service is ultimately paid out of lease cash flows, which puts lease duration, renewal risk, and debt amortization front and center. Lease terms which are longer than debt maturities are preferred to satisfy refinancing risk concerns given uncertainty over renewals. Some bonds will use amortizing structures to guarantee that principal and interest is covered by lease payments. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. In countries where online transactions have a significant market share, online and offline prices are closely related and online prices may lead offline as the demographic of computer-literate, middle-class, cash-rich and time-poor consumers to which online retailers sell are less price-sensitive than the average consumer. As purchasing habits change, these online price series capture prices and changes in product information and can provide real time information on consumer behaviour. In our reasoning, higher prices are not the consequence of excess demand, but they are the cause of an erosion of domestic demand. There is therefore no need for policy to tighten. It is possible that we underestimate the impact of the ongoing supply shock on core inflation, in particular if the disruption spreads more widely to supply chains, as the initial price shock translates into a volume shock, i.e. if supply of critical material produced in the Persian Gulf impairs production more widely. That would make for an even more stagflationary environment, not just for a more inflationary environment. So it would likely not change the conclusion that inflation causes a destruction of demand (making it less likely to be sustained) and is not the consequence of an excess of demand. The price shock is likely to remain just that, a one-off shock (as incidentally was the 2022 shock, albeit on a different scale). The other difference of course with 2022 is the initial setting of policy, which was very expansionary then, and is towards the top end of neutral now. records.text: Second part of report title David Wilson, Head of Metals Strategy | BNP Paribas Singapore Branch 9 China’s construction sector still a demand drag: Direct use of copper in construction (excluding energy infrastructure) accounts for roughly 10% of China’s refined copper demand. The sector remains in contraction despite signs of a modest improvement in home-buying earlier in the last year, and we do not expect construction to return as a positive copper demand driver. Energy infrastructure / grid investment accounts for c.55% of China’s copper demand, but growth slowing: China’s energy infrastructure spending slowed sharply in 2025 to RMB639.5bn, up only 5.1% y/y, the lowest growth rate in four years. The slowdown reflects not only China’s maturing energy networks but also the impact of investment in ultra-high-voltage grids becoming increasingly aluminium-centric. China’s refined copper production continues to surge: While China’s copper demand has been slowing, domestic refined production has continued to grow rapidly, up 7.5% in January–February 2026, after reaching full-year output of 14.7Mt in 2025. The slowing demand and strong domestic refined production have driven a dramatic downtrend in China’s net refined copper imports, down almost 50% y/y over the first two months of 2026, following a 15% y/y decline in 2025. records.text: The High-Grade Beat 27 April 2026 Citi Research 2 The first wave of tariff announcements on Canada and Mexico in February 2025 marked a fundamental shift in economic relations and foreign trade between the US and the rest of the world. Since then, a number of geopolitical incidents have flared up and put to the forefront fears of large outflows from US corporates. As we have mentioned before, a significant rotation out of US corporates is structurally impractical. Based on a combined view of the primary U.S. and European IG corporate indexes, US-domiciled issuers account for 65% ($7.5 trillion) of the total $11.6 trillion outstanding. Within the >15-year maturity segment of the U.S and European corporate IG markets, a critical segment for insurance and pension investors globally, 81% is issued by U.S. corporations, and a staggering 94% of debt is denominated in USD. Thus, global investors seeking long-duration credit exposure have no viable alternatives at scale, reinforcing the structural barriers to a widespread rotation away from U.S. assets. The result of this stickiness in demand has been a consistent 15-month inflow from overseas investors. Figure 1 highlights how, since December 2024, appetite from abroad has shown no signs of slowing down. As we highlighted before in The High-Grade Beat - Following the foreign flows, tariff rates announced during April 2025 had a low correlation with the level of flows from May-July. Year to date, bank securities holdings are $141bn higher, including $78bn in USTs, extending the sector's solid demand for securities in 2025. Meanwhile, deposits fell by $32bn, and we expect the next H.8 release to show a larger drop, as has typically been the case around the tax deadline ($200bn in 2025 and $256bn in 2024, for example). On the foreign side, Japanese investor demand was broadly flat in the week to April 17, an improvement compared with the prior four-week average, at $5bn in net foreign note and bond sales. In February, we had also suggested that even a “hawkish” Governing Council would find it difficult to hike policy rates without some solid evidence that the price shock is morphing into endogenous inflation dynamics, because an inevitably controversial decision (tightening policy when growth slows) would require a broad consensus in the Council, and that there would be enough members who would be reluctant to take action without hard evidence. Given the long time it may require for such evidence to surface if it ever does (e.g. genuine “second round effects” , acceleration of wages or higher frequency of price reset by firms), we concluded that the bar for a hike remained reasonably high through this year. Gradual bond-to-swap catch-up expected as FX remains strong: The asset-swap spread looks too wide after a sharp rally in the local curves, creating an appealing risk-reward setup for a potential convergence of the bond curve with the swap curve, underpinned by a consolidating swap curve and a strong peso. Since the start of the Middle-East conflict, movements in the asset-swap have been driven largely by the beta of the swap curve, which tends to be more volatile than the bond curve during rapid risk-on/risk-off shifts. With a better external risk sentiment and the market largely pricing out the conflict-related risk premiums— evidenced by the 10y TIIE-F trading only 26bp above its pre-conflict level despite oil prices surging over 10%—we anticipate that the bond curve could close the gap with the swap curve gradually, supported by a strong peso (favoring the bond more) and a likely consolidation of the swap curve as long as there are no meaningful developments in the Middle East in the short term. records.text: Alex Swade Michael Metcalfe 27 April 2026 Classification: Premium Material 1 Insights Information Classification: General FX Execution Insights – Re - risking and re - rating FX conditions Figure 1: FX movements and rate expectations Figure 2: Volume (5-day, percentiles) Weekly Insights: In the two-months since the beginning of the conflict in Iran movements in FX markets have shown little correlation with movements in interest rate expectations (Figure 1). records.text: 2 Insights SPOTLIGHT VIEWS: USD, EUR, GBP…MOST OF THE DM Clear as mud: Central banks are in the spotlight, with no less than nine major policy makers reporting from the DM (4) and EM (5) this week. And while there is nothing priced into any of the DM curves, investors will clearly be looking for insight into how central bankers are thinking about the surge in energy prices. For the moment, it appears as if investors have abandoned the transitory lens that policy makers often apply to these situations, with terminal expectations rising across all developed economies . Nonetheless, it will take policy makers moving from their well-worn playbook of patience in the face of growth concerns for many of the hike expectations to come to fruition. The impetus for action is clear after 5+-years of above target inflation, although we are not convinced that central banks will easily reach this conclusion. So, while we are on the lookout for moderated views, which may be viewed dovishly, our MKT MediaStats readings on hawkish/dovish tone signal that they have no choice but to fulfil the market’s tightening mandate. We think that most central banks will try and keep optionality, although expected hikes from the ECB, BOE and Norges at their mid-summer meetings may need a bit of groundwork to be laid at this meeting. records.text: Noel Dixon 28 April 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General BoC Preview: Staying on hold for more evidence The Middle East War has added complexity to the Bank of Canada's already challenging circumstances. Despite signs of economic recovery, households continue to face significant hurdles such as rising living costs, debt strain from upcoming mortgage renewals, and persistent uncertainty in the labour market. Against this backdrop, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s fiscal policy is intentionally expansionary in the near term, which may influence the BoC’s decisions on interest rates. The energy shock caused by the conflict has pushed headline inflation above the BoC’s projection from its January monetary policy report (MPR), though Q1’s average median and trimmed mean inflation were slightly lower than expected. Overall, the BoC has room to pause at its April 29 meeting to further assess inflation trends. Nevertheless, we anticipate the BoC will raise its inflation outlook while keeping its growth forecast unchang ed in the upcoming April MPR. In our view, inflationary pressures will intensify over the medium term as fiscal measures take effect, the labour market strengthens, and wages rise. Eventually, these factors should prompt the BoC to adopt a more hawkish stance, which, along with favourable positioning, supports a positive outlook for the CAD in the medium term. records.text: M Idea 2 1Q26, up from 13% in 1Q25. • Mapping the Midterms...We recently collaborated with our policy strategists on a report looking at equity market impacts from the Midterm elections. From our perspective, the policy vectors likely most important for markets through the end of President Trump’s term will remain under his control (foreign policy, tariffs, de-regulation). It's worth noting that earnings growth today far surpasses the historical precedent in second year periods of Presidential cycles (a 10% differential). This speaks to a point we’ve long been partial to, which is that the path of the business cycle ultimately outweighs the policy agenda. • Back to the Future…With equity markets rebounding at a historic pace from our preferred entry point (6300-6500 for the S&P) and re-embracing many of our core themes (rolling recovery/rebalancing, capex/capital markets boom and broadening earnings growth), investors are now asking if the market will give them another chance to add risk. With passive investors still under-risked, pullbacks are likely to be shallow, in our view, with remaining risks for the market still centered on the Fed transition/uncertainty around inflation, which could lead to short, yet manageable spikes in bond volatility and/or funding market stress.

As we argued in introduction, we cannot rule out that the closure of the Straits extends for a very long time, but we cannot rule out either an explicit or implicit understanding between belligerents that allows shipping traffic to resume. From a monetary policy perspective, this translates into an impossibility to conclude whether the ongoing shock is lasting or temporary. Yet, in the face of a supply shock, the classical central banking textbook says that one must wait and make this pronouncement before deciding to react, or not. If the Straits were to reopen quickly, having hiked rates now could be seen ex post as a panic move and be detrimental to credibility. If, however, the price shock were to prove more prolonged, a delay in responding could also lead to a loss of credibility, but only if inflation expectations de-anchor in the meantime. On balance, the latter risk strikes us as much lower than the former, because (1) there is still no evidence currently of de-anchoring of expectations and (2) the six-week gap between policy meetings is short enough to allow the ECB to adjust policy “in a timely manner” should any such evidence arise. records.text: In addition, accelerated share repurchases (ASR) represent a potential avenue for management to signal confidence in the growth outlook amid disruption risk. Many companies consistently repurchase shares as a form of returning cash to shareholders. However, ASR programs can underscore a firm’s commitment to actually repurchasing shares in the near term. Managements often use ASRs to signal that they believe the company is undervalued and future growth prospects are strong. Academic research generally finds positive share price reactions to the announcement of ASRs that are also larger than reactions to traditional repurchase program announcements3. Executive Summary US credit has largely faded both the Middle East shock and the recent move higher in rates, ending April at 80/270/489bps in IG/HY/LL, tighter than at the start of March across all three indices. Over the same period, 10y yields have crept higher by nearly +45bps to just under 4.40% at the time of this writing, driven by higher real rates (+26bps). Notably, however, the repricing higher in inflation expectations has accelerated, with over half of total widening in 10y breakevens since the start of the conflict (+19bps) happening in the past week alone. records.text: Euro Area Watch | 30 April 2026 3 FX: balanced approach remains the sweet spot Michalis Rousakis MLI (UK) michalis.rousakis@bofa.com The ECB’s April meeting offered little new for FX. While the press conference carried some hawkish undertones, this was largely expected. By its end, EUR/G10 was marginally lower (except vs the Scandies) compared with pre-statement levels, though overall moves were limited. From here, a balanced ECB approach remains the ‘sweet spot’ for the EUR. Rate hikes delivered in response to bad (inflation) reasons are less supportive than hikes delivered in response to good (growth) reasons, even when well calibrated. For EUR-USD, the Fed remains the more important driver. Our economists expect two Fed cuts later this year (September, October). An ECB focused on protecting its inflation credentials vs a Fed that prioritizes the labour market could support EURUSD further out. Such an outcome would also reduce FX hedging costs for European investors. That said, the ECB avoiding an over-reaction remains key. Historical analogues provide a note of caution, even if the current macro backdrop differs materially (see also the report, EUR/USD: Navigating stagflationary risks 7 Apr '26 ). Beyond central banks, we remain cautious on EUR-USD in the near term, looking for 1.14 in Q2. records.text: Asia Economic Weekly | 30 April 2026 3 Thailand in Focus Pipat Luengnaruemitchai Kiatnakin Phatra Securities Lattakit Lapudomkarn Kiatnakin Phatra Securities (Link to full report: Thailand Viewpoint: Maneuvering in a tight fiscal space) Thailand’s recent sovereign outlook revision from Negative to Stable by Moody’s serves as a vital endorsement of the country’s external resilience and manageable debt profile. However, this window of stability is being immediately stress-tested by a "stagflationary squeeze" as Brent oil prices remain sustained above US$90/bbl. As a net energy importer, Thailand faces a direct conflict between maintaining fiscal discipline and protecting domestic purchasing power. The Oil Fuel Fund, the primary stabilization vehicle, has seen liabilities surge to approximately Bt60bn. While the government has successfully reduced subsidy commitments from Bt20 per liter to Bt7 per liter by compressing refinery margins and allowing gradual price pass-throughs, the margin for policy error is narrowing. A renewed spike in energy prices would test the government's resolve to hold the line on fiscal consolidation versus providing targeted support for households. Debt Dynamics: The 70% Warning Light The Medium-Term Fiscal Framework (MTFF) prepared at the end of last year indicated that public debt is on a trajectory to approach the 70% legislative ceiling by 2028. records.text: y rate as of the April meeting (%) Source: Federal Reserve Board, BofA Global Research BofA GLOBAL RESEARCH Uncertainty + resilient data = hawkish hold The Fed will remain firmly on hold at its April meeting. The inflation outlook is arguably as cloudy as it was at the time of the March meeting. Meanwhile, the recent labor data show resilience and potentially some green shoots. The big question around the FOMC statement is whether it will indicate that risks to the policy path are two-sided. We think it won’t, but it’s a close call. We anticipate only one dissent. Chair Powell should sound hawkish in what will probably be his last presser. We’ll be listening for a few things. First, how open-minded is he to rate hikes? Second, how does he balance war-driven inflation against downside risks to growth/labor? Third, what does he say about Kevin Warsh’s comments last week and his own future at the Fed? We look for a limited rates market reaction to the policy communication and believe the market will have a high bar to price hikes. We also expect no change in Fed operational tools. The April FOMC meeting is also unlikely to be a major event for the USD, but risks skew marginally bullish if Chair Powell reiterates his more hawkish tone from March. From our coverage, leaching accounts for a large share (>25%) of production for GLEN, FCX and ANTO (Fig 14), although we believe all three are in relatively strong positions through acid production elsewhere in the portfolio ( FCX and GLEN) and limited spot exposure (ANTO). Boliden and Aurubis are large producers of sulphuric acid through their smelting assets. Based on our estimates, >300 ktpa of copper production could be at risk from acid shortages. n The aluminium market is facing a real Supply Shock; if the flow of alumina into the ME does not improve soon, aluminium prices could spike even higher (potentially over >$4k). The region produced ~6.8 mt in 2025 (Fig 18), making up ~9% of global production.
